title: The woman no one could see
hookLine: an empty hermitage, a curse, and the way back built into it
carry: prayashchitta: penance, and a way back

cards: With the sacrifice done, the hermits at Siddhashrama have a plan. King Janaka of Mithila is holding a great sacrifice, they tell Rama, and he keeps a bow there you should see.

So they walk north for days, and every evening the sage tells stories: how the Ganga came down from heaven, how the ocean was churned. Just outside Mithila, they pass an old hermitage. Lovely, but completely empty.
No smoke from the fire, no voices. Whose was this, Rama asks, and why is no one here?

teach.b: This was the hermitage of the great sage Gautama, Vishvamitra tells him, and his wife Ahalya. One day, while Gautama was away, Indra, king of the gods, came to Ahalya disguised as her husband.
Here the versions part, and it matters which you're hearing. In Valmiki's telling, Ahalya sees through the disguise and agrees anyway, out of curiosity about the king of the gods.
Some later tellings say she was fully deceived. Either way, Gautama comes home, sees Indra slipping out in the sage's own form, and curses them both.
To Ahalya he says: you will stay here for thousands of years, unseen by any living being, living on air, lying in ash, doing penance.
And in the same breath: when Rama comes and you welcome him as a guest, you'll be free. Here's the Hindu teaching tucked inside.

teach.h: PRAYASHCHITTA: PENANCE, AND A WAY BACK.
teach.b: The tradition has a word for it: prayashchitta, penance, atonement. A wrong has real consequences; that's karma. But in Hindu teaching a consequence isn't the end of a person.
Penance works it through, and the way back is part of the story from the start.

teach.h: HER YEARS IN THE ASH: TAPAS.
teach.b: Ahalya's years in the ash aren't wasted. They're her tapas, and tomorrow you'll see them make her shine. And here's what surprises people.
Some Hindus, as part of their morning prayers, recite a short verse remembering five honored women, the panchakanya.
The first name in it is Ahalya. Not hidden away. Remembered first.
So the empty hermitage isn't empty. Someone has been there the whole time, doing her penance, waiting for a guest. Go in, Vishvamitra tells Rama.
Tomorrow, what happens when he does.

how: Ahalya is honored in Hindu tradition as one of the panchakanya, five women whose names some Hindus recite in a well-known morning verse; her story is told very differently across tellings, and discussions of it often turn on those differences.

o: Gautama's wife, cursed to wait unseen for Rama
a hermit who lives alone near Janaka's city
a goddess who guards the road to Mithila

prayashchitta: penance works it through, and Gautama's curse named its own end.

games.q: sam hears Ahalya's story and says 'so she's the bad guy, right?' by the tradition, what fits?
o: no: she does her penance, she's freed, and some Hindus say her name first each morning.
yes: in Hinduism one big wrong marks you for good.
it doesn't matter; the story is really about Indra.
games.why: prayashchitta: the wrong is real, the penance is real, and so is the way back. that's why her name is remembered, not hidden.

practice: If you pray, you can do what some Hindus do each morning and say the five names slowly: Ahalya, Draupadi, Sita, Tara, Mandodari. If you don't, think of someone paying a long time for a mistake, maybe yourself.
Don't retell the mistake. Just picture the way back already open, and on each breath out let a little warmth go their way.

wordCard.voice: Ahalya restored. Gautama's wife, doing penance unseen until Rama comes, and remembered first among five honored women.

orig.note: Sanskrit ahalyā: the wife of the sage Gautama, one of the five honored women of the panchakanya verse.

carryVoice: Your line: prayashchitta, penance, and a way back. Even Gautama's curse named its own end. Until tomorrow.
